what_it_does: Memory Protection Keys (MPK) is a hardware feature that lets a program divide its own memory into labeled domains and quickly grant or revoke access to each domain without asking the operating system — useful for isolating sensitive data inside a single application. The catch is that the instruction that changes those permissions (called WRPKRU) forces the processor to stop and finish all previous work before proceeding, which is slow when an application switches domains frequently. SpecMPK allows the processor to execute this permission-change instruction speculatively and out of order, while carefully blocking any subsequent memory access to a newly unlocked region from being finalized until the permission change itself is committed — ensuring that transient (short-lived) permission windows cannot be exploited by speculative-execution attacks similar to Spectre.
